newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE-Pill's path to approval in Japan still rocky.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pill's path to approval in Japan still rocky.

text.p: Japanese women, denied the birth control pill for more than 30 years, may have to wait a while longer as the latest prospect of government approval again appears in danger of running into the sand.

Strong expectations that the pill would finally be given the green light have yielded to uncertainty after some members of a public health committee involved in the review process said its approval, by discouraging condom use, could lead to the spread of AIDS.

Japan remains the only major industrialised country to ban the pill for contraceptive purposes. Low-dose contraceptives are banned altogether while high and medium-dose pills may be only prescribed for menstrual disorders.

Hopes for approval of the pill grew when former Health Minister Naoto Kan said last July that he expected a favourable decision this year. These hopes then blossomed when the first of three ministry committees required to give their blessing said the pill was safe and effective.

While charged by the second committee with debating what effect the legalisation of the pill would have on the spread of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), the public health committee has no power to approve or disapprove the pill.
PILL PROPONENTS FEAR ANOTHER U-TURN

But the possibility of a negative report has worried women's groups and pharmaceutical firms who fear further delays or even a repeat of 1992 -- when the ministry dramatically reversed a decision to lift the ban, citing concerns about Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS).
"It's just like 1992 again. The whole discussion is moving away from the pill to STDs," said a representative of one of the pharmaceutical firms, who asked not to be named.
Critics question the make-up of the public health committee, whose members include no specialists on the pill, and argue that linking the issues of contraception and AIDS is wrong.

The second committee will not make any decision until the committee on public health has come up with a report for which the timetable is very unclear. "Scientific studies have shown that there is no relation between AIDS and the pill. Even so, there are people who assert this -- a stance that shows little regard for women's health," said Akiko Domoto, chief representative of the Sakigake Party and a member of the Upper House.
AIDS SCANDAL MAKES BUREAUCRATS WARY
Critics also say the Health Ministry is hyper-sensitive about AIDS.

In a scandal that has shocked Japan, senior bureaucrats have gone to trial on charges of professional negligence for approving blood products that were tainted with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which causes AIDS, and which infected haemophiliacs.
Now no committee wants to make a decision that could lead to a rise in AIDS cases, no matter how remote the possibility, they say.
"The ministry is shoving reponsibility left and right, too scared to take the responsibility for anything," said the representative of one of the pharmaceutical companies.

Proponents of the pill add that while concerns about AIDS have taken the spotlight this time, worries about the country's low birthrate and the championing in some quarters of conservative sexual mores were also working to delay approval.
THE PILL COULD HIT JAPAN'S ABORTION INDUSTRY

The pill has gone through tortuous cycles of coming within inches of official approval before being turned back. Concerns over sexual mores, side effects and AIDS have over the years all played their part in keeping it off the market.
The reluctance of some physicians, who fear loss of income from abortions, to actively campaign for the pill's introduction has also been blamed.
Family planning experts say that the advent of the pill should reduce the number of abortions in Japan.
While official figures estimate the number at under 400,000 a year, some studies put it much higher, saying nearly 30 percent of Japanese pregnancies end in abortion.
IGNORANCE AND INDIFFERENCE ALSO PLAY A PART
But experts also admit that a large part of the pill's failure to make it in into pharmacies alongside other contraceptives in Japan has been overwhelming indifference to the issue.
In addition, pharmaceutical firms have not campaigned for the pill's introduction, reluctant to oppose the Health Ministry, which has wide regulatory powers.
"It's fear of the ministry," said the representative of one of the firms.
Coverage of the pill by domestic media is cursory, and domestic surveys show that many Japanese women are ignorant about the pill.
The latest poll on the subject in the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper last year showed that around 40 percent of Japanese women questioned said they either knew nothing or very little about the pill.
